One small change to the actor update makes RL work for flow policies on real robots, VLAs, and even image models. Here's QF3 from UC Berkeley and Amazon FAR, explained in 4 minutes!!!

A lot of robots today run on flow policies. A flow policy turns random noise into an action by following a learned velocity field, one small step at a time. Think of it as diffusion for actions. You normally train one by imitation, on a dataset of demonstrations.

Reinforcement learning is harder, because there's no dataset. The robot only has its own attempts in a replay buffer. You train a critic, Q, to score actions. The most direct way to improve the policy is then to follow the critic's gradient: predict where the flow lands in one step, and push it uphill on Q.

The catch is that if that prediction lands far from anything in the buffer, the critic is guessing. When it overestimates, the policy chases a fake peak and training falls apart which is not at all what we want!

QF3's fix is to clip the policy's velocity so its prediction stays close to the replay action, where the critic can be trusted. Past the clip, the gradient is simply masked out. It's one actor update, with a standard critic and no extra networks.

The results are pretty promising 
• Fine-tuning a pretrained bimanual VLA (ABC-VLA) with only LoRA adapters on its flow action head, VLM frozen. In the side-by-side episodes, the QF3 policy finishes bottles-in-bin 1.8× faster and plates-in-dish-rack 2.1× faster than the base policy. 
• Full fine-tuning on the robomimic Square, Tool Hang and Transport tasks. 
• Humanoids trained from scratch: they dropped QF3 into FastTD3 unchanged and deployed on real hardware for velocity tracking and motion tracking. Yes, it dances. On motion tracking it reached the same performance about 10× faster in wall-clock time than FPO++, on a single GPU. 
• The same update fine-tunes Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium. Each prompt is a one-step episode, and the PickScore reward model plays the critic.

I like this because it's the most direct way to use a critic, made safe with a one-line idea: only trust the gradient where the critic has seen data. Teleoperated demonstrations are slow and expensive, and a policy that RL can make faster and better after imitation is a big deal.

AI VIDEO CREATORS, HAVE YOU EVER CONSIDERED SELLING SHORT ADVERTISING JINGLES TO BUSINESSES? 😭🔥

Not every advertisement needs a long voiceover.

Sometimes, a short, memorable musical message can make a brand's content more interesting.

And when you combine AI music tools with AI video creation, you can explore an entirely different service.

Let me show you how.

Imagine a restaurant launching a new meal combo.

Instead of creating an ordinary product advertisement, you develop a catchy 15-second musical commercial.

The food is beautifully presented.

There's a fun, original jingle.

The restaurant's name is clearly communicated.

And the video ends with the actual offer and ordering information.

Now imagine doing something similar for:

- Fashion brands
- Restaurants
- Schools
- Retail stores
- E-commerce businesses
- Event organizers

Here's how to start.

STEP 1: Learn how advertising jingles are structured.

A good jingle should communicate a brand's message, not just sound entertaining.

STEP 2: Practice writing short, original advertising lyrics.

STEP 3: Use appropriately licensed music and audio tools to develop your sound.

STEP 4: Combine the music with a well-directed AI video advertisement.

STEP 5: Build three demonstration commercials for fictional brands.

Then research businesses that might be interested in this style of advertising.

You can offer:

A 15-second musical advertisement.

A 30-second brand commercial.

Or a collection of short promotional jingles.

Check the commercial rights for every music and voice-generation tool you use. Don't imitate famous artists or copy recognizable songs without permission.

Here's the opportunity:

YOU CAN COMBINE STORYTELLING, MUSIC, VIDEO PRODUCTION, AND ADVERTISING INTO ONE CREATIVE SERVICE.

The more clearly you define what you're offering, the easier it becomes for a potential client to understand its value.

A robot's movement can teach us more than you might think. 🤖

Imagine controlling a robot arm on your computer screen.

You move it toward an object, adjust its position, and try to pick it up. Every movement is part of the task.

Now imagine those actions being recorded as data that can help train robots.

That's the interesting idea behind simulation-based robot training.

With @axisrobotics Robotics, people can interact with simulated robots and demonstrate how different tasks should be performed.

These demonstrations can be captured as trajectories basically, records of how the robot moved while completing a task.

Why does that matter?

Because robots need examples of how to perform physical actions. 
Human demonstrations can provide useful training data without requiring every contributor to own a physical robot.

Of course, a simulation isn't the same as the real world. Robots still need to handle unexpected situations and be tested outside virtual environments.

But making robot training more accessible could open the door for more people to contribute to the future of physical AI.

Sometimes, teaching a robot starts with something as simple as showing it how a task is done. 🦾

We’re sharing more of our research, starting with our paper on outcome-routed post-training for diffusion language models.

Many standard RL methods are difficult to apply reliably to diffusion language models. Our approach avoids policy likelihood ratios and combines reward-based learning with teacher guidance.

Tool-calling accuracy (BFCL) rose from 53.55% to 88.6%, without increasing the model’s size.

The result: a more effective way to post train diffusion language models for new capabilities.

Our team will present the work at the NeurIPS 2026 DiffuLM. https://t.co/zTjk2to0hm

Diffusion models are complicated to RL because many training methods that work for AR don't work well for diffusion.

We present a methodology for post-training diffusion models that combines reward-based learning with teacher guidance.

The result is more effective way to post train diffusion language models for new capabilities.
